voice.refText: Twice a week, you sell your plasma, the pale part of your blood. It's the most the law allows. That's the band. A thin strip you wear across your forehead. While you sleep, it lends your brain to a company. And it pays you, by the hour.

Boss.describe: A smooth male baritone: a hotel owner in his fifties who smells money. Slightly oily, pleased with himself, clipped and greedy, a showman's grin in the voice.

Flatmate.describe: A bright, warm female voice: a woman of about twenty-six, the listener's flatmate. Mezzo, quick and chatty, always mid-story, a laugh under the words, casual modern English.

Guest.describe: A loud, jolly male baritone: a tourist in his sixties off a night coach. Round and booming, delighted, a laugh ready behind every word.

Student.describe: A high, sharp female voice: a girl of about seventeen in a school uniform. Quick, cheeky and clever, a lawyer's question in a teenager's mouth.

Nurse.describe: A brisk, clear female mezzo: a hospital nurse in her forties. Fast, practical and unfussed, a clipboard voice.

Surgeon.describe: A dry, deep female alto: a surgeon in her fifties who has rehearsed too much. Slow, puzzled and very tired, a deadpan question.

Kid.describe: A high, bright child's voice, about ten years old. Quick, natural and lively.

Teacher.describe: A tired, firm female alto: a schoolteacher in her forties. Brisk, unimpressed, used to being obeyed.

Bride.describe: A soft, calm female mezzo: a woman of about thirty in a wedding dress. Warm, settled and amused, sure of herself.

Judge.describe: A flat, heavy male bass: a judge in his sixties. Grave, slow and final, three words like a door shutting.

Traveller.describe: A crisp, polite female mezzo: a businesswoman in her thirties who speaks nine languages. Light, precise and kindly pitying, a well-travelled ease.

lines.text: Boss: Staff first.
lines.say: [greedy, delighted, a grin in it] Staff first.
lines.speaker: Boss

lines.text: Flatmate: So my brother, right...
lines.say: [bright, quick, mid-story, laughing already] So my brother, right...
lines.speaker: Flatmate

lines.text: Flatmate: ...and then he dropped it.
lines.say: [bright, the punchline, waiting for the laugh] ...and then he dropped it.
lines.speaker: Flatmate

lines.text: One night for her. One year for you. And you spent it learning to juggle.
lines.say: [amused, close, a shrug on the last sentence] One night for her. One year for you. And you spent it learning to juggle.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So what if you lived a year, every night?
lines.say: [thrilled, leaning in, a lift on every night] So what if you lived a year, every night?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Every night, a lifetime of skills. Every morning, a face like that. That's what you win. What you lose is your head start, the day anyone else gets a cable.
lines.say: [gleeful on the win, a quick cold turn on the loss] Every night, a lifetime of skills. Every morning, a face like that. That's what you win. What you lose is your head start, the day anyone else gets a cable.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The rule, once. Plug in at bedtime, and your mind runs about a thousand times faster. A night out here is a year in there.
lines.say: [clear, exact, brisk, enjoying it] The rule, once. Plug in at bedtime, and your mind runs about a thousand times faster. A night out here is a year in there.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: In there, a town of other sleepers, a job, weather, four seasons. You remember all of it. Your body ages one night.
lines.say: [exact, warming on the list, a wink on the last sentence] In there, a town of other sleepers, a job, weather, four seasons. You remember all of it. Your body ages one night.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You bring back only what's in your head. No things, no news. And once you're in, you stay till the alarm. Remember that.
lines.say: [measured, each limit its own beat, the last two words pointed] You bring back only what's in your head. No things, no news. And once you're in, you stay till the alarm. Remember that.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The thousand isn't ours. An economist who studies uploaded minds, Robin Hanson, guessed one would run about a thousand times human speed. A year is 8,760 hours. At a thousand times, about eight and three-quarter hours. One night.
lines.say: [curious, brisk, the sum landing flat and sure] The thousand isn't ours. An economist who studies uploaded minds, Robin Hanson, guessed one would run about a thousand times human speed. A year is eight thousand seven hundred and sixty hours. At a thousand times, about eight and three-quarter hours. One night.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And you've got work in the morning.
lines.say: [dry, a shrug, half a smile] And you've got work in the morning.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Why a cable? In rats, the sleeping brain replayed a learned route six to seven times faster than the run itself. But a dream runs at about real speed. Lucid dreamers counting to ten take about as long as they do awake. So it takes a plug.
lines.say: [curious, quick, answering the viewer before they ask, a small reveal on the last sentence] Why a cable? In rats, the sleeping brain replayed a learned route six to seven times faster than the run itself. But a dream runs at about real speed. Lucid dreamers counting to ten take about as long as they do awake. So it takes a plug.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Night one. A town at dawn. A paper sun racing the sky. A bakery job. A winter. A piano teacher with a grey head, and a back room full of radios and lamps in pieces. You help. You've got time.
lines.say: [wonder, quick cuts, offhand and smug on the last two sentences] Night one. A town at dawn. A paper sun racing the sky. A bakery job. A winter. A piano teacher with a grey head, and a back room full of radios and lamps in pieces. You help. You've got time.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day three hundred in there. Your hands get it right.
lines.say: [proud, slowing, a drumroll in it] Day three hundred in there. Your hands get it right.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Flatmate: So my brother...
lines.say: [easy, over cereal, same as every morning] So my brother...
lines.speaker: Flatmate

lines.text: Flatmate: Since when?
lines.say: [stunned, a laugh breaking in it, genuinely asking] Since when?
lines.speaker: Flatmate

lines.text: Flatmate: Who's Haruko?
lines.say: [baffled, a little offended, quick] Who's Haruko?
lines.speaker: Flatmate

lines.text: Haruko runs the bakery. In there. Michel Siffre came out of a cave with no clock, after about two months, 25 days behind the calendar. You've come out the other way: a year ahead, and a year out of date.
lines.say: [deadpan, then a story told low, the gap landing on the last four words] Haruko runs the bakery. In there. Michel Siffre came out of a cave with no clock, after about two months, twenty-five days behind the calendar. You've come out the other way: a year ahead, and a year out of date.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You wanted applause. You got a question and a wrong name. Fine. You've got all the time in the world.
lines.say: [dry, then breezy, a dare in the last sentence] You wanted applause. You got a question and a wrong name. Fine. You've got all the time in the world.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Night two, you learn to cook. You make her eggs.
lines.say: [gleeful, quick, proud] Night two, you learn to cook. You make her eggs.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Flatmate: I hate eggs.
lines.say: [flat, bored, pushing the plate away] I hate eggs.
lines.speaker: Flatmate

lines.text: She told you yesterday. For you, a year ago. Night three, you go in for the lottery numbers. Here's the thing. The town knows nothing you don't. Its newest newspaper is whatever the last sleeper read before bed. Inside, the stock market is a year of very clever people arguing about last Tuesday.
lines.say: [deadpan, then conspiratorial on 'here's the thing', a laugh under the last sentence] She told you yesterday. For you, a year ago. Night three, you go in for the lottery numbers. Here's the thing. The town knows nothing you don't. Its newest newspaper is whatever the last sleeper read before bed. Inside, the stock market is a year of very clever people arguing about last Tuesday.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So, nights four to seven: languages. The hard ones take about 2,200 class hours for native English speakers at the US diplomats' school. You've had four whole years. Four languages, at a working level.
lines.say: [brisk, impressed, building] So, nights four to seven: languages. The hard ones take about two thousand two hundred class hours for native English speakers at the US diplomats' school. You've had four whole years. Four languages, at a working level.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Midnight. A coach party. Forty guests, four languages, one desk, and you.
lines.say: [thrilled, quick, a showdown announced] Midnight. A coach party. Forty guests, four languages, one desk, and you.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Guest: Is he real?
lines.say: [a stunned guest, delighted, to the room] Is he real?
lines.speaker: Guest

lines.text: Bigger than the piano. Then you go home and can't open the door.
lines.say: [smug, then the deadpan drop] Bigger than the piano. Then you go home and can't open the door.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The code. Four digits you typed yesterday. For you, a year ago. Sleep is when the brain files the day, and one small, famous experiment, in 1924, decided that forgetting is mostly the new rubbing out the old. A year of new, every night. Last night never stood a chance.
lines.say: [dry, exact, a story told low, the last sentence flat and finished] The code. Four digits you typed yesterday. For you, a year ago. Sleep is when the brain files the day, and one small, famous experiment, in nineteen twenty-four, decided that forgetting is mostly the new rubbing out the old. A year of new, every night. Last night never stood a chance.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Flatmate: Right. So my brother...
lines.say: [cheerful, toast in hand, letting you in] Right. So my brother...
lines.speaker: Flatmate

lines.text: And you can't remember how it starts. Problem one: you're not forgetting in there. You're forgetting out here.
lines.say: [dry, the problem numbered and landed with a raised eyebrow] And you can't remember how it starts. Problem one: you're not forgetting in there. You're forgetting out here.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Your boss has been watching the counter.
lines.say: [dry, a warning in it, half amused] Your boss has been watching the counter.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Boss: Triple.
lines.say: [greedy, flat, decided] Triple.
lines.speaker: Boss

lines.text: By midnight there's a queue down the street.
lines.say: [brisk, rising, trouble coming] By midnight there's a queue down the street.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Your boss sells every coil before dawn. By the end of the week, the whole city is plugging in, and your hotel has a waiting list to the harbour.
lines.say: [brisk, rising, a showman's wink on 'every coil'] Your boss sells every coil before dawn. By the end of the week, the whole city is plugging in, and your hotel has a waiting list to the harbour.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: A student plugs in the night before the exam and sits it with a year of revision. Next morning, the exam board bans sleeping the night before.
lines.say: [quick, amused, building] A student plugs in the night before the exam and sits it with a year of revision. Next morning, the exam board bans sleeping the night before.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Student: Define sleeping.
lines.say: [deadpan, a teenager who has read every law book, bored] Define sleeping.
lines.speaker: Student

lines.text: Why not become a surgeon in a week? One tries. She rehearses one operation ten thousand times by breakfast. But the town only knows what the sleepers brought in, and the scan waiting outside is eight hours newer.
lines.say: [answering the viewer, brisk, then the turn landed cold] Why not become a surgeon in a week? One tries. She rehearses one operation ten thousand times by breakfast. But the town only knows what the sleepers brought in, and the scan waiting outside is eight hours newer.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Nurse: New scan.
lines.say: [brisk, matter of fact, holding it up] New scan.
lines.speaker: Nurse

lines.text: Surgeon: Newer than what?
lines.say: [panicked, a year of confidence draining in three words] Newer than what?
lines.speaker: Surgeon

lines.text: 'On my desk by morning' now means a year's work. Every boss means it. By Friday, that's the minimum, and nobody's impressed.
lines.say: [dry, mock-weary, the joke landing on impressed] 'On my desk by morning' now means a year's work. Every boss means it. By Friday, that's the minimum, and nobody's impressed.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Schools ban it under sixteen. The kids plug in anyway, and turn up to class as forty-year-olds in uniform.
lines.say: [gleeful, quick] Schools ban it under sixteen. The kids plug in anyway, and turn up to class as forty-year-olds in uniform.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Kid: Miss. We've done this.
lines.say: [a child's voice with a middle-aged weariness, patient, flat] Miss. We've done this.
lines.speaker: Kid

lines.text: Teacher: Sit down.
lines.say: [sharp, rattled, holding the room] Sit down.
lines.speaker: Teacher

lines.text: Every wedding in the city: the bride plugs in the night before and thinks it over for a year.
lines.say: [warm, amused, a held breath at the end] Every wedding in the city: the bride plugs in the night before and thinks it over for a year.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Bride: I do. Still.
lines.say: [calm, certain, a smile in it] I do. Still.
lines.speaker: Bride

lines.text: Then the courts.
lines.say: [quick, a raised eyebrow] Then the courts.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Judge: Three nights.
lines.say: [grave, formal, a gavel in the voice] Three nights.
lines.speaker: Judge

lines.text: The prisoner expected a long weekend. He walks out three years older, grey-eyed, and thanks the court. He asks to stay in. Nobody gets to. The alarm's out here. So is his bladder.
lines.say: [amused, then answering the viewer, flat and cheerful on the last sentence] The prisoner expected a long weekend. He walks out three years older, grey-eyed, and thanks the court. He asks to stay in. Nobody gets to. The alarm's out here. So is his bladder.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The morning train. Every face a year older in mind, and smug about it. Nobody on a phone. They've read everything. Two people who argued at dinner sit side by side. Only one is still angry. The other forgave her a year ago and has written a book about it.
lines.say: [amused, slower, savouring it, the last sentence delivered deadpan] The morning train. Every face a year older in mind, and smug about it. Nobody on a phone. They've read everything. Two people who argued at dinner sit side by side. Only one is still angry. The other forgave her a year ago and has written a book about it.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And all of them went into the same town you did. Inside is filling up.
lines.say: [awed, a door opening, the last sentence slower] And all of them went into the same town you did. Inside is filling up.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Then a traveller checks in. In nine languages.
lines.say: [deadpan, the drop on nine] Then a traveller checks in. In nine languages.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Traveller: Only four?
lines.say: [polite, pitying, a guest who means well] Only four?
lines.speaker: Traveller

lines.text: A year's work is the minimum now. Your head start lasted exactly as long as the crate. And your boss has been doing sums. A cable is worth a car. Then a flat. Then a street.
lines.say: [dry, the edge gone, then dread climbing with each sum] A year's work is the minimum now. Your head start lasted exactly as long as the crate. And your boss has been doing sums. A cable is worth a car. Then a flat. Then a street.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Boss: Staff last.
lines.say: [greedy, cold, the same grin turned round] Staff last.
lines.speaker: Boss

lines.text: He's not wrong. Out here, you're the guy who can juggle.
lines.say: [deadpan, a shrug, a laugh under it] He's not wrong. Out here, you're the guy who can juggle.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You could quit. Then you lose the hatch too. He has the only cables in the city, padlocked to a hook you can see from your chair.
lines.say: [dry, trapped, the last clause slow and bitter-funny] You could quit. Then you lose the hatch too. He has the only cables in the city, padlocked to a hook you can see from your chair.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So you nap at the desk. A twenty-minute nap is about two weeks in there. You wake up humming a whole opera.
lines.say: [sly, answering the viewer, gleeful on the opera] So you nap at the desk. A twenty-minute nap is about two weeks in there. You wake up humming a whole opera.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Boss: No naps.
lines.say: [flat, final, slapping a tag on] No naps.
lines.speaker: Boss

lines.text: Problem two. A thousand people in this hall are living a year tonight. You're doing eight hours and the rota.
lines.say: [dry, the problem numbered, the last word flat] Problem two. A thousand people in this hall are living a year tonight. You're doing eight hours and the rota.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Count it anyway. Thirty nights. Thirty years in there, one month out here. And the town has the whole city in it now.
lines.say: [awed, slow on the reveal, then quickening] Count it anyway. Thirty nights. Thirty years in there, one month out here. And the town has the whole city in it now.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: An email you get at six is answered at seven, after a year's thought, and the answer is a book. A fashion lasts a century in one outside afternoon. The word everyone says on Monday night is a grandparent's word by Wednesday.
lines.say: [delighted, brisk, a laugh under it] An email you get at six is answered at seven, after a year's thought, and the answer is a book. A fashion lasts a century in one outside afternoon. The word everyone says on Monday night is a grandparent's word by Wednesday.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Three in the morning. The only two people in the city having a normal night.
lines.say: [tender, quiet, a smile in it] Three in the morning. The only two people in the city having a normal night.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Flatmate: So. My brother.
lines.say: [settling in, warm, finally getting to tell it] So. My brother.
lines.speaker: Flatmate

lines.text: You finally hear the middle. It's a terrible story. It takes four minutes. You've been putting it off for thirty years.
lines.say: [tender, amused, the last sentence fond] You finally hear the middle. It's a terrible story. It takes four minutes. You've been putting it off for thirty years.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: She gets to the kettle. You look at its lead, and remember the back room.
lines.say: [a spark, low, conspiratorial] She gets to the kettle. You look at its lead, and remember the back room.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Your boss knows about the piano and the languages. He doesn't know about the radios. You've had his cable in your hands every night for a month. In there, you spent a year drawing it from memory with a man who fixes lamps. It's a lamp cord with opinions.
lines.say: [sly, quickening, a heist being laid out, deadpan on the last sentence] Your boss knows about the piano and the languages. He doesn't know about the radios. You've had his cable in your hands every night for a month. In there, you spent a year drawing it from memory with a man who fixes lamps. It's a lamp cord with opinions.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Why not just buy one? A cable costs a street. You earn a desk.
lines.say: [answering the viewer, deadpan, quick] Why not just buy one? A cable costs a street. You earn a desk.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Next night shift. The desk lamp's cord. The kettle lead. The taped-over spare socket under your old hatch.
lines.say: [hushed, quick, each item a beat, a thief's checklist] Next night shift. The desk lamp's cord. The kettle lead. The taped-over spare socket under your old hatch.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Footsteps on the stairs.
lines.say: [panicked, a whisper] Footsteps on the stairs.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Flatmate: Sir. So my brother, right...
lines.say: [bright, loud, blocking the stairs, stalling for her life] Sir. So my brother, right...
lines.speaker: Flatmate

lines.text: Boss: Not now.
lines.say: [irritated, trying to get past] Not now.
lines.speaker: Boss

lines.text: Flatmate: He bought a kettle.
lines.say: [earnest, urgent, as if it matters enormously] He bought a kettle.
lines.speaker: Flatmate

lines.text: He's stuck. She can do four minutes. You need two. Your hands have had thirty years.
lines.say: [breathless, counting down, the last sentence sure] He's stuck. She can do four minutes. You need two. Your hands have had thirty years.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And that year inside? You spent it teaching. Every sleeper in the town, the whole design, from a kettle lead and a lamp cord. Only what's in your head comes back. A design is in your head.
lines.say: [triumphant, quick, the last two sentences slow and landed] And that year inside? You spent it teaching. Every sleeper in the town, the whole design, from a kettle lead and a lamp cord. Only what's in your head comes back. A design is in your head.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: By morning, the whole city wakes up knowing how to build one. By lunch, there isn't a kettle lead left in the city. By dinner, a cable costs a kettle. Your boss's crate goes out on the pavement with a price card crossed out eleven times.
lines.say: [gleeful, accelerating, relishing every 'by', a laugh on eleven] By morning, the whole city wakes up knowing how to build one. By lunch, there isn't a kettle lead left in the city. By dinner, a cable costs a kettle. Your boss's crate goes out on the pavement with a price card crossed out eleven times.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: By the weekend, three governments ban kettles. By Monday, they un-ban them. The ministers plugged in.
lines.say: [deadpan, quick, the last sentence a shrug] By the weekend, three governments ban kettles. By Monday, they un-ban them. The ministers plugged in.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Night one hundred and twenty-three. You've outlived the longest verified human life. And you're still on the night shift.
lines.say: [awed, then dry on the night shift] Night one hundred and twenty-three. You've outlived the longest verified human life. And you're still on the night shift.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Keep this up ten years and you'll have lived more than three and a half thousand. Unroll it. English from about a thousand years ago, the English of Beowulf, can't be read today without study. Keep going.
lines.say: [awed, slow, each step a beat, the last two words a dare] Keep this up ten years and you'll have lived more than three and a half thousand. Unroll it. English from about a thousand years ago, the English of Beowulf, can't be read today without study. Keep going.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The one who climbs out of that pod won't understand a word the one who climbed in said. You won't understand you. Your boss will still want the rota.
lines.say: [hushed, mind-boggled, then deadpan on the rota] The one who climbs out of that pod won't understand a word the one who climbed in said. You won't understand you. Your boss will still want the rota.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And the city? Every night now, it lives a year. It designs in a week what used to take a century. Nobody's impressed by that either.
lines.say: [awed, quick, a shrug on the last sentence] And the city? Every night now, it lives a year. It designs in a week what used to take a century. Nobody's impressed by that either.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Then the hatch next to yours opens.
lines.say: [a hush, the turn, a smile hidden in it] Then the hatch next to yours opens.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Flatmate: Tell me tomorrow.
lines.say: [smug, heavy-lidded, delighted with herself, your line in her mouth] Tell me tomorrow.
lines.speaker: Flatmate

lines.text: Tomorrow's a year away. For once, it isn't yours.
lines.say: [amused, warm, the last clause slow] Tomorrow's a year away. For once, it isn't yours.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Boss: Two plugs.
lines.say: [greedy, delighted, the same grin as the opening] Two plugs.
lines.speaker: Boss

lines.text: So, who gets your second plug? Tell us in the comments. And if you'd have done the same, hit like and subscribe.
lines.say: [direct, easy, a grin in it] So, who gets your second plug? Tell us in the comments. And if you'd have done the same, hit like and subscribe.
lines.speaker: narrator
